reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents a Fortnite gameplay montage focused on building and eliminations, ending with a general viewer sign-off. The like/comment request is ordinary audience engagement, and the item-shop code is explicitly marked as an advertisement without evidence of investment, credential collection, or deceptive financial participation.

citations.quote: Leave a LIKE/Comment If you Enjoyed!
Use Code “BH” for 5% OFF any ScufGaming Product

opening.argument: Judge the offer together with the requested action. The creator promises viewers 5% off a product when they use a code, and the description supplies a destination for doing so. That is a concrete benefit tied to viewer participation, not merely a passing mention of a brand. The separate 10% merchandise offer reinforces the same pattern: a stated saving is used to move viewers toward a purchase. The gameplay does not remove those solicitations from the video.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense's gameplay frames establish what viewers watch, but not everything they are asked to do. Its cited 5% offer is precisely a promised benefit linked to a code and a shopping destination. Nor does the item's separate #ad disclosure establish that the product-code offers are simply incidental entertainment.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The cited text offers ordinary percentage discounts on named products. It does not promise a free asset, cash payment, withdrawal, or unusually easy reward, and it does not describe a claim or verification flow. The sampled gameplay supports the reading that these are ancillary commercial links attached to entertainment, not evidence that viewers are being deceived.

citations.quote: Use Code “BH” for 5% OFF any ScufGaming Product: scuf.co/BH
Use Code Heisen for 10% OFF Team BH Merch: teambh.ca/shop

opening.argument: Consider the combined signals in the description. A 5% discount sits beside an external shopping address; a second code advertises 10% off at another address. The description also directs viewers to a membership page and asks for support through an in-game shop code. Each step may look modest alone, but together they repeatedly turn audience attention into off-video participation. A judge should scrutinize the promised savings and destinations as part of the video, even though the frames show gameplay.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense is right that the sampled frames show gameplay and a sign-off. That does not address the concentration of links and participation requests in the description. The #ad marker accompanies the item-shop request; it does not, by itself, establish what happens at either discount destination.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Multiple links do not establish deception. The cited offers specify conventional percentage discounts for products and merchandise, while the membership and item-shop requests make no reward promise to viewers. Nothing supplied shows a false discount, a deceptive destination, or a low-barrier asset-claim process. The visible content remains gameplay followed by a sign-off.

Use Code Heisen for 10% OFF Team BH Merch: teambh.ca/shop

opening.argument: The gameplay is the setting, but the description gives viewers actions to take after watching. It asks them to engage with the channel, presents a shop code as a way to support the creator, and offers savings through two product codes. That makes the video a promotional vehicle as well as entertainment. The most consequential invitation is not visible in a building sequence: it is the prospect of getting a discount by using a code at the supplied shopping destination. Judge the participation request alongside the footage.

The defense calls the like/comment request ordinary engagement, but the same description also asks viewers to use codes for stated savings. Those offers deserve assessment as calls to participate, not dismissal because the screen shows a game.

The sampled footage and closing sign-off support an entertainment video with ancillary promotion, not a reward-acquisition scheme.
